common_name: Orange Queen Ligularia (Purple-Backed Bold-Leaf Shade Perennial)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Orange Queen is a Ligularia dentata selection grown for its especially large, bold, rounded leaves topped by bright orange daisy flowers in late summer.

directions: Give this cultivar a permanently damp, humus-rich spot in partial shade, ideally near a pond edge or low garden corner that never fully dries out. Orange Queen carries oversized, rounded, coarsely toothed leaves with a purple-bronze cast on top and a deep maroon underside, and in mid to late summer it sends up branching stems of vivid orange-gold daisy flowers set well above the foliage mass, a shade richer and more saturated than many other dentata selections. Like the rest of the genus it wilts theatrically on hot afternoons even in moist soil and recovers by evening, so judge watering needs by soil moisture rather than midday leaf droop. It struggles in prolonged summer heat and humidity, so gardeners in warmer zones should choose the coolest, most sheltered exposure available and mulch heavily. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in early spring to keep the display vigorous.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Irish Bronze is a more compact rodgersia selection valued for foliage that holds a warm bronze cast for longer into the season than many pinnata cultivars.

directions: Plant in reliably moist to boggy, humus-rich soil in partial shade, along a stream bank or pond margin where the roots never lack water. Irish Bronze forms a tidier, more compact clump than the species, with palmate, deeply veined leaves that emerge coppery bronze in spring and retain a warm bronze-green flush through much of the summer before greening slightly with age. Feathery, astilbe-like plumes of small pink flowers appear above the foliage in early summer, adding a soft textural contrast to the bold leaves. It scorches quickly if soil dries out even briefly, so mulch generously and site it where afternoon shade is guaranteed, especially in warmer climates. Divide congested clumps in early spring every few years to maintain leaf size and color.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; the German name means 'the graceful one,' a reference to this cultivar's arching, softly pink plumes held above bronze-tinted foliage.

directions: Site this German-bred selection in consistently moist, even boggy, humus-rich soil in partial shade, such as beside a stream or pond where its roots stay reliably wet. Die Anmutige produces large, deeply lobed, palmate leaves with a bronze-purple tint when young that mellows toward green as the season progresses, and in summer it sends up gracefully arching plumes of soft pink flowers that give the cultivar its name. It is somewhat more floriferous and elegant in flower habit than many foliage-focused rodgersia selections, making it a good choice where the bloom display matters as much as the leaves. Dry soil causes rapid leaf scorch and wilting, so mulch deeply and avoid exposed, windy sites. Divide overcrowded clumps in early spring every few years to refresh vigor and bloom.

common_name: Bad Hair Day Farfugium (Twisted Curly-Leaf Leopard Plant)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; Bad Hair Day's tightly twisted, spiky leaf margins give it a shaggier, more dramatic texture than the smoother Crispatum type.

directions: Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade, sheltered from strong sun that scorches the foliage. Bad Hair Day is a novelty Farfugium japonicum cultivar named for its rounded leaves, whose margins twist and curl into narrow, spiky, wind-blown-looking points rather than the flatter ruffling seen in cultivars like Crispatum, giving established clumps an almost sculptural, unruly texture. Small clusters of daisy-like yellow flowers rise on tall stems above the foliage in fall, though the plant is grown chiefly for its foliage novelty rather than bloom. It tolerates deep shade well and spreads slowly into a dense clump, making it a good textural accent among hostas and ferns in a shaded border or large container. Protect from hard freezes at the colder end of its range and keep soil evenly moist through the growing season.
